headline: Wi-Fi 7 Delivers 46 Gbps Speeds with Wider Channels & MLO
summary: The latest Wi-Fi standard, IEEE 802.11be, offers double the channel width and simultaneous multi-link operation for significantly improved performance.
details: Wi-Fi 7, also known as IEEE 802.11be, has been certified under the Wi-Fi Alliance's Wi-Fi CERTIFIED 7 program, launched January 8, 2024. The finalized specification was published by the IEEE in July 2025. Many devices purchased in the last year or two likely already support this new generation.

Key advancements in Wi-Fi 7 include 320 MHz channels, which double the widest channels of previous generations, enabling multi-gigabit speeds. This is made possible by regulators opening up the 6 GHz band for unlicensed use.

Mandatory for certification is Multi-Link Operation (MLO), allowing devices to transmit and receive simultaneously across multiple bands and links. This boosts throughput, reduces latency, and ensures traffic continuity even when one band experiences congestion.

Wi-Fi 7 also introduces 4K QAM, which packs 20% more data into each transmission compared to Wi-Fi 6's 1024 QAM. Theoretically, Wi-Fi 7 can reach speeds of up to 46 Gbps, a fivefold increase over Wi-Fi 6's ceiling of 9.6 Gbps.

While theoretical maximums are impressive, real-world speeds are naturally lower. However, Wi-Fi 7 retains crucial features from Wi-Fi 6, including WPA3 security, full backward compatibility, and the efficiency-first design that prioritizes consistent performance in crowded airspaces.

For most households, the upgrade to Wi-Fi 7 will be noticeable not just as a higher speed number, but as a network that maintains its speed even when numerous devices are connected and active simultaneously. This focus on consistency addresses a key user pain point.

headline: AI coding cost measurement timed out, not reported as $0
summary: A 30-second timeout in AI coding cost measurement failed to record any cost, potentially skewing aggregate data. The issue has been addressed with an increased timeout and clearer error reporting.
details: An AI coding cost measurement tool experienced a timeout after 30 seconds, but instead of recording a cost, it produced no record at all. This is distinct from a measurement that successfully completes and registers a zero cost.

The underlying measurement process could complete in approximately 36 seconds, but the caller terminated it after 30 seconds. The error message was vague, making it difficult to distinguish between a measurement failure and a timeout.

Failing to measure something and measuring it as zero are not the same. If multiple failed measurements are silently converted to $0, the resulting average cost can appear lower than the evidence supports.

A fix has been implemented, increasing the default timeout from 30 seconds to 180 seconds and making the timeout error explicit. This allows for clearer distinction between a measurement command failing on its own and the caller terminating it.
With the increased timeout, measurement processes can now complete, return a protocol payload, and persist their results, ensuring that data is not lost or misrepresented as zero.

This issue highlights the importance of accurately representing measurement states, as collapsing all failures into zero can destroy crucial information about what actually happened, a principle applicable beyond AI coding costs.
